title: The Occupancy Illusion: Why a Fully Booked December Doesn't Guarantee a Profitable One for Accommodation Operators
linkedin:
A fully booked December feels like the best run of the year for an accommodation business.

The margin underneath it often tells a different story.

Once online travel agency commissions are taken out, often in the order of fifteen to twenty per cent, the average daily rate that actually lands in the bank account is well below the rate on the listing.

Then there's staffing. A property running at ninety per cent occupancy over Christmas and New Year needs more housekeeping turns, more laundry, faster maintenance response, all on the days penalty rates are highest. The marginal cost of filling the last ten per cent of rooms is frequently higher than the revenue those rooms bring in once wages and consumables are counted properly.

The number worth tracking through the peak isn't how full the calendar looks. It's what each booking actually nets once the channel fee and the labour cost are counted against it.

The businesses that come out of January with a clear year ahead are usually the ones that built that discipline into the season before it started, not the ones waiting to see how the numbers land.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

If you run accommodation along the Queensland, New South Wales or Victorian coast, you're probably watching your December and January booking calendar fill up right now, and it probably looks like the best stretch of the year ahead.

Here's the pattern we see every peak season with accommodation operators: a fully booked property doesn't always mean a fully profitable one. Booking platform commissions, often fifteen to twenty per cent, come out before a dollar reaches the bank account. Peak season staffing, housekeeping, laundry and maintenance, costs more per room over Christmas and New Year because it falls on the days penalty rates are highest. And the admin that gets pushed aside during the rush, channel reconciliation, repricing, leave accruals, usually resurfaces as a surprise in February rather than a plan.

None of this means the peak season is a bad one. It usually isn't. It just means occupancy is the wrong number to watch on its own. The number that actually matters is what each booking nets once the channel fee and the labour cost are taken into account.
